items.prompt: Priya fixed the outage; Marcus shipped a smaller feature. Why did Elena make the stronger case for Marcus?

She believed his work was worth more than the outage fix
She had forgotten that Priya's outage fix ever happened
items.explanation: Elena respected Priya. The gap came from what she could cite, not from how she valued the work.

items.prompt: Which statement matches how this unit separates visibility from quality?

Visibility is a measure of how loudly and how often a person talks about the work
Visibility is whether decision-makers know of the work, not how good it is
items.explanation: Quality belongs to the work itself. Visibility is about whether the work reached the people deciding.

items.prompt: In the calibration room, who has to argue for Priya?
choices: Priya herself, who presents her own quarter to the managers
Elena, her manager, speaking for her while Priya is absent
Marcus, who compares his quarter with hers in front of everyone
items.explanation: Priya is not in the room. Her case is only as strong as what Elena can say on her behalf.

items.prompt: What does 'citable' mean for a piece of work?
choices: Someone can point to a specific, checkable record of it later
Someone remembers hearing that the work went well overall
Someone feels confident that the person is generally strong
items.explanation: Citable work comes with something concrete to point at, such as a document or a number.

items.prompt: Priya's fix was posted in a Slack thread that four people read. What was the main problem with that?
choices: The fix itself was too small to matter to anyone reading it in the thread
Posting in a thread is against the usual rules of the team
Almost no decision-makers ever saw it, so it left nothing to cite
items.explanation: The work was strong, but it never reached a place where Elena could draw on it later.

items.prompt: Which is true of good work that never reaches a decision-maker?
choices: It still counts fully because quality always speaks for itself
It may count for nothing in the room where decisions get made
It counts more, because modest people are trusted more
items.explanation: A room can only weigh what it has been told. Unseen work carries no weight there, however good.

items.prompt: Elena pauses, then gives a vaguer answer about Priya. What does the vagueness signal?
choices: She lacks concrete material, not that she lacks regard for Priya
She secretly disagrees that Priya deserves a promotion at all
She thinks the other managers will not care about the answer
items.explanation: Vagueness comes from having nothing specific in hand, not from a lack of belief.

items.prompt: Marcus told his manager about his work in several places. What did this give Elena?
choices: A reason to distrust him for talking about himself so often in meetings
Proof that his work was harder than anything Priya did
More detail she could repeat when asked about him
items.explanation: Repeated telling put his month into Elena's memory in detail. That says nothing about difficulty.

items.prompt: Two engineers each deliver equally strong results this quarter. Their manager can recite a dated summary of one person's work and only a vague impression of the other's. What is the most likely result in a closed-door review?

Both get equal backing because quality outweighs the available detail
The person with the summary gets the more confident backing
The person with the summary gets weaker backing because it looks rehearsed
items.explanation: Advocacy runs on what the advocate can cite. With equal quality, detail decides who is argued for more firmly.

Doing good work and hoping it speaks for itself

items.explanation: The record carries the information, so you do not need to announce your greatness.

items.explanation: Self-promotion declares your own value directly. The other two state checkable facts.

items.prompt: What does 'credit-sharing' mean?

Letting teammates take the credit for work you actually did
Splitting any praise you receive evenly with everyone present
items.explanation: Credit-sharing is accurate naming of who did what, including you.

items.prompt: What is a 'decision point'?
choices: A moment when you decide which tasks you will work on next
A moment when a team votes on where to hold its next group meeting
A moment when someone with authority is forming a judgment your work matters to
items.explanation: Decision points are where information about your work can change an outcome.

items.prompt: Why does credit-sharing make your own role more believable?

It signals an accurate account rather than a self-serving one
It lowers the bar for what counts as your own real contribution
items.explanation: Listeners trust accounts that include other people's real contributions.

items.prompt: Why do both extreme approaches lose?

Silence draws suspicion from managers, and loud claims are rarely noticed at all
Both approaches are noticed too much and draw unwanted attention
items.explanation: One approach fails by reaching nobody and the other by being discounted when it does.

Both read as modest because both are sharing their results
The first risks sounding boastful; the second offers checkable evidence

A reminder that Priya has never complained about anything
items.explanation: A named outcome with a record is both checkable and easy to repeat.

items.prompt: In calibration, a manager says 'my report is outstanding' and another says 'my report cut order errors from forty a week to six; here's the writeup.' Why does the second claim usually carry more weight?

It proves that the second report works much harder than the first
It can be checked or concretely pictured by the room
It is longer, and longer claims are taken more seriously
items.explanation: Both managers may be sincere. Only one has given the room something to hold onto.

items.prompt: Do the tactics make up for work that isn't good?
choices: No, the work still has to be good for the tactics to help
Yes, a good record can replace weak work if it is well written
Yes, so long as the timing is right near a big decision
items.explanation: None of this manufactures value that isn't there.

items.prompt: Sam, unprompted, tells the team in a demo that Priya's fix is the reason checkout has been stable. If Priya said the same sentence herself, what would change?
choices: The facts become less accurate when coming from the person who did the work
The facts reach more people because the demo audience is larger
The facts stay the same, but the listener trusts the source less
The facts stay trusted equally because the source is irrelevant
items.explanation: The source changes how the same information is received, because self-interest is discounted.
items.reference:
Four ways to make evidence travel
📝 Documentation: dated, checkable facts
📣 Others amplify: a third party repeats them
🤝 Credit-sharing: name your role and theirs
📅 Timing: send before the decision

Why: each tactic moves the record to the decision-maker without extra first-person claims.
items.learnMore:
Four tactics, one idea

Each tactic lets the evidence carry the information, rather than your own declarations of your worth.

Common mistake

Using one tactic in a way that undoes another, such as asking a colleague to praise you in public. That swaps evidence for a staged claim.
items.reflection: Which of the four tactics would feel most natural in your current work, and which would feel most awkward? What does that tell you?

items.prompt: A speaker says 'we shipped the fix' when they led it. Which tactic have they misapplied, and what is the cost?
choices: Credit-sharing, because the vague 'we' hides who drove it
Timing, because the update came at a rather unplanned moment
Amplification, because nobody else repeated the claim
Documentation, because the update was spoken instead of being written down
items.explanation: Real credit-sharing names both your role and a collaborator's. A vague 'we' loses your part.

Letting others amplify the work in conversation
Sharing credit while staying visible as the driver
Timing around an actual decision point
items.explanation: The facts are identical. What differs is whether someone is forming a judgment that needs them.

items.prompt: What was Priya's running doc written like?
choices: Long personal stories about what the quarter felt like
Bullet points ranking her work against her teammates'
Short, factual lines in the voice of a postmortem report
items.explanation: A factual voice keeps the doc reading as evidence.

items.prompt: Which word is absent from the 'after' column of Priya's table?
choices: Dates, numbers and links to the original writeups
"I" and adjectives praising her own work
Names of the systems or products she worked on
items.explanation: The entries avoid first-person claims and self-praise.

items.prompt: What makes a sentence 'evidence' rather than a declaration?
choices: It makes a checkable claim about the real world
It is written in a longer and more formal style
It is placed in a document instead of a chat message
items.explanation: Evidence can be verified. A declaration asks for trust.

items.prompt: Which is the better line for the doc?
choices: "Incredible quarter: I basically rescued checkout single-handedly"
"So proud of the checkout work I led, it really went well"
"Checkout outages: 3 before the fix, 0 since. Writeup linked"
items.explanation: Only the first states a verifiable change.

items.prompt: Why does Priya write down small things as well as big ones?
choices: Small entries impress readers more than a single big one
A running record means nothing has to be recalled from memory
A long list is taken as proof that she is busy all year
items.explanation: The doc turns scattered work into a record she or Elena can cite.

items.prompt: Is the difference between evidence and declaration mostly length?
choices: No, it is whether the claim is checkable or about her own value
Yes, evidence is always shorter than a declaration
Yes, evidence is always longer than a declaration
items.explanation: Length is not the test. Checkability is.

items.prompt: Why did Priya describe the new hire's progress as a fact?
choices: Facts about other people are always easier to write down
Facts about the new hire matter more than her own work
The fact shows impact without her praising herself
items.explanation: A concrete outcome speaks for her mentoring.

items.prompt: What happens to a doc full of 'I'm proud of' lines?
choices: It reads as especially trustworthy because it is written down
It reads as a declaration wearing a document's formatting
It reads as neutral because documents are always objective
items.explanation: Format does not turn a claim about worth into evidence.

items.prompt: Which pair of lines about the same project best shows the evidence versus declaration difference?
choices: "Refund wait time: 9 days to 3 days" versus "Refunds now take three days"
"I made refunds so much faster" versus "I made refunds a lot faster"
"Refunds now take three days" versus "Refund wait time: 9 days to 3 days"
"Refund wait time: 9 days to 3 days" versus "I made refunds so much faster"
items.explanation: Only the first pair contrasts a checkable fact with a claim about the speaker's own effect.
items.reference:
Declaration versus evidence
❌ 'I basically saved checkout'
✅ 'Outages: 3 in six months before, 0 in three months since'
The difference: can a reader check it?

Why: evidence makes a claim about the world; a declaration makes a claim about your own value.
items.learnMore:
The postmortem voice

A postmortem states what happened and what changed, without commentary about who deserves praise. That is the voice that makes a record read as evidence.

Common mistake

Dropping the checkable part. A tidy sentence with no number, date or link is still just a claim.
items.reflection: Take one thing you did this month. Can you describe it as a change in the world that someone else could verify?

items.prompt: Priya's running doc is full of dated, factual lines but she never shares it or tells anyone it exists. What is the likely result?
choices: Strong benefit, because the doc exists for anyone who looks
Little benefit, because someone still has to know to look
Strong benefit, because documents are noticed on their own
Negative effect, because unseen documents count against her
items.explanation: A doc with no distribution is barely better than none.

items.prompt: How did Priya make Sam's mention of her work more likely?
choices: She kept a factual doc that Sam could read and then recall
She asked Sam to praise her fix at the next team demo
She sent Sam a note listing the reasons she deserved credit
items.explanation: A findable, factual doc lets a peer speak specifically without being prompted.

items.prompt: Who said Priya was the reason checkout had been stable?
choices: Priya, in her own speech to the team
Elena, in a message sent to the director
Sam, unprompted, during a team demo
items.explanation: The visibility came from Sam's unprompted sentence.

items.prompt: What did Priya do in the meeting where Sam spoke?
choices: She corrected Sam's account to add more detail about herself
She said thanks and simply moved on
She listed her other recent accomplishments in response
items.explanation: She let the third-party mention stand without adding to it.

items.prompt: Which sentence names both roles well?
choices: "I led the root-cause investigation, and Sam's testing showed the fix held"
"We fixed the checkout issue this quarter, as a team effort"
"I fixed the checkout outages, basically single-handedly"
items.explanation: It names Priya's role and Sam's specific contribution.

items.prompt: What does 'we fixed it' hide?
choices: Who attended the planning meetings
Who wrote the final summary of results
Who actually led all of the work
items.explanation: A vague 'we' makes Priya's own role disappear.

items.prompt: What does 'I did it, basically single-handedly' erase?
choices: The timeline of the work
Collaborators' real contributions
The numbers behind the result
items.explanation: Over-claiming erases others and damages trust.

items.prompt: Why are listeners sensitive to over-claiming?
choices: They tend to notice when an account leaves out other people's work
They tend to prefer long accounts over short, factual ones
They tend to ignore the speaker's role entirely in stories
items.explanation: Accurate accounts include other people.

items.prompt: What is 'amplification' in this context?
choices: Increasing the volume of your own announcements
Posting your update in more channels than usual
Someone else repeating real facts about your work
items.explanation: Amplification works because the source is not you.

items.prompt: Priya's teammate Sam sees her running doc and, weeks later, mentions her fix unprompted. Priya then sends Sam a note asking him to mention it again next month. What is the likely effect?
choices: The second mention reads as stronger, since Sam is now prepared
The second mention reads the same, since the facts are unchanged
The second mention may read as staged, costing credibility
The second mention reads as modest because Priya stayed quiet
items.explanation: Solicited amplification is often detectable and loses the unprompted quality that made it trustworthy.
items.reference:
Credit that stays accurate
🙈 'We fixed it' hides who led it
🙊 'Single-handedly' erases Sam
✅ 'I led the investigation; Sam's testing showed the fix held'

Why: accurate naming of both roles keeps you visible and makes the account more believable.
items.learnMore:
Naming roles precisely

Specific credit makes a statement checkable. It also signals that the speaker is describing events rather than managing an image.

Common mistake

Using 'we' or 'I' by habit. Each one quietly erases someone, either you or a collaborator.
items.reflection: Recall the last time you described a team result aloud. Whose contribution did you name, and whose went unmentioned?

items.prompt: At an all-hands, Priya says 'I led the investigation, and Sam's testing showed the fix held.' Why is this stronger than saying 'We fixed it'?
choices: It states her role clearly and gives an accurate account including Sam
It makes the list of contributors longer than the other version
It places the focus on Sam instead of on her own contribution
It avoids using the word 'I', which listeners find off-putting
items.explanation: The specific naming defeats both invisibility and over-claiming.

items.prompt: When did Priya send Elena her one-pager?
choices: The day after the calibration meeting had ended
About a week before the calibration meeting
On the first day of the quarter's work
items.explanation: She sent it while Elena was still building her case.

items.prompt: Was the one-pager new information to Elena?
choices: No, Elena already had access to the doc all along
Yes, it contained results Elena had never been shown
Yes, it replaced an earlier doc that had been deleted
items.explanation: The same facts landed differently because of the timing.

items.prompt: Why does timing matter?
choices: Elena only reads documents that arrive near a deadline
Elena forgets documents sent earlier than a week before
Elena was actively forming a judgment that needed the information
items.explanation: Information used during a decision is input; earlier it is background.

items.prompt: What happens if the one-pager arrives the day after the decision?
choices: It becomes more persuasive because the outcome is known
It becomes a historical footnote instead of an input
It is automatically added to the next decision's file
items.explanation: Timing is not optional for the information to influence the outcome.

items.prompt: Which is a failure mode of the doc?
choices: Writing it but never letting anyone know it exists
Writing it in a plain, factual voice about outcomes
Keeping it short so that a busy reader can skim it
items.explanation: Documentation with no distribution is barely better than none.

items.prompt: What does a doc full of 'I'm the reason' lines turn into?
choices: A balanced record that reads as especially honest
A neutral log that nobody feels the need to question
A first-person highlight reel that reads as declaration
items.explanation: Voice decides whether it reads as evidence.

items.prompt: Which line of the note to Elena sounds suitably low-key?
choices: "Please make sure everyone in the room hears about all of this"
"No need to reply, just wanted you to have it before the meeting"
"I hope you will remember how much I did this quarter"
items.explanation: The note offers input without pressing for anything.

items.prompt: For a bigger audience, such as a director who has never met Priya, what is a question the unit asks?
choices: Which tactic carries the most weight as the audience grows
Whether to stop documenting once enough people know her
Whether to skip the timing tactic when the audience is large
items.explanation: The extension question asks how the tactics change with the audience.

items.prompt: Priya's doc has existed all quarter. Elena skimmed it in month one and moved on. A week before calibration, the one-pager from it arrives. Why does the second reading do more work?
choices: Elena has now forgotten the earlier version of the doc
Elena now gives more weight to anything that is shorter
Elena now sees the information for the very first time
Elena is now actively building an argument that needs this input
items.explanation: The facts are the same. The need for them is what changed.
items.reference:
Priya's timeline
📄 Running doc exists all quarter
📅 One-pager sent a week before calibration
✅ Elena uses it as live input
❌ Sent after the decision: a footnote

Why: the same information is input when a judgment is forming, and history afterwards.
items.learnMore:
When information does work

Being available is not the same as being used. A decision-maker uses what is in front of them at the moment they decide.

Common mistake

Assuming that because a document exists, it has been seen. Delivery at the right moment is part of the tactic.
items.reflection: Think about a decision coming up for someone you work with. What information could help them, and when would it be most useful for them to receive it?

Solicited praise, so the facts look staged to the reader
